einzeiler: The story of how Home Depot became the world's largest home improvement retailer.
kurzfassung: Home Depot revolutionized the hardware industry by pioneering the giant warehouse format with unmatched product selection and everyday low prices. Founded by retail veterans after sudden corporate firings and backed by visionary financing, the company scaled rapidly across North America. Despite a challenging leadership era in the 2000s, Home Depot returned to its cultural roots and built a dominant omnichannel empire.
stichpunkte: Home Depot was founded in 1979 by Bernie Marcus, Arthur Blank, Ken Langone, and Pat Farrah after being ousted from their previous employer.
The founders introduced a revolutionary large-format warehouse concept that offered vastly more product choices and lower prices than traditional hardware stores.
Ken Langone engineered the company's early funding rounds and took Home Depot public in 1981 during a severe macroeconomic downturn.
The business model relied on powerful scale economies, direct-to-store manufacturer relationships, and hiring experienced trade professionals as store associates.
By 1989, Home Depot surpassed Lowe's to become the largest home improvement retailer in America.
Bob Nardelli's tenure as CEO brought Six Sigma operational rigor and rapid store expansion, but alienated employees and cratered customer satisfaction.
Frank Blake took over in 2007, halted new store openings to focus on store productivity, and aggressively bought back shares while building out digital fulfillment.
Today, Home Depot operates over 2,400 stores, generates $165 billion in annual revenue, and maintains a dominant position in serving both DIY consumers and professional contractors.

clips.hook: Beating Apple's investment return since IPO
clips.text: An initial investment in Home Depot at its IPO outperformed a simultaneous investment in Apple, compounding at nearly 25 percent annually over 45 years.

clips.hook: The warehouse retail revolution that terrified founders
clips.text: The creation of early warehouse-style discount clubs threatened to completely destroy traditional retail business models unless adopted by hardware stores.

clips.hook: Going public as a tiny four-store chain
clips.text: Home Depot completed its initial public offering with a tiny market capitalization while operating only four stores in Atlanta during a brutal economic downturn.

clips.hook: Massive share buybacks that failed to move the stock
clips.text: Despite authorizing billions of dollars in share repurchases, the company's stock price remained completely stagnant during a specific management era.

clips.hook: Grooming the CEO of your primary competitor
clips.text: A former Home Depot executive eventually left the company to become the chief executive officer of their chief rival, Lowe's.

beschreibung:
The Home Depot's founding story is like an Avengers movie… if the Avengers got fired, went broke, and stacked empty paint cans ten feet high to look legitimate. After being unceremoniously fired from their previous hardware chain at ages 48 and 35, Bernie Marcus and Arthur Blank took the words of their New York banker Ken Langone (who had also just accidentally caused their firings) to heart: they'd just been "kicked in the ass with a golden horseshoe.” They proceeded to author the greatest compounding story in American retail history, helped by some legendary cameos along the way from Sol Price, Jamie Dimon, and Ross Perot (to name a few). And the ending is as good as any superhero film: from its 1981 IPO to today, The Home Depot has been the single highest-returning equity in the entire US stock market — higher than Apple, Microsoft, Berkshire Hathaway, and everything else!
